findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns
findings.body: The legacy write runs in a goroutine but its context is derived from ctx, the incoming request context. net/http cancels a request's context when ServeHTTP returns, which happens right after Storage.Create returns and the response is written. The 10s timeout wrapper is built on that already-canceled context, so Legacy.Create typically fails with context canceled before it writes anything. Legacy writes will be lost for most requests, silently, which defeats the purpose of mode 3. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The background write should detach from the request context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere
findings.body: The goroutine only feeds a boolean into a duration metric and drops the error. The base code logged legacy failures with the object attached. Now a failed legacy create (including a timeout) produces no log line and no error detail, so the unified/legacy divergence this mode is meant to guard against is invisible to operators. The same omission exists in Delete (line 113), Update (line 140) and DeleteCollection (line 166).

findings.title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered per object
findings.body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object serialization. Two quick successive operations on the same playlist (for example update then update, or update then delete) can reach the legacy store out of order, leaving legacy with the older state while unified storage holds the newer one. Nothing detects or repairs this, and the 10s timeout makes it more likely. This needs either per-key serialization or an explicit, documented eventual-consistency guarantee with tests.

findings.title: Legacy update recomputes the change from its own state instead of writing the unified result
findings.body: The base code wrapped the Storage.Update result in updateWrapper so the legacy store received exactly what unified storage produced. This version passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update. objInfo.UpdatedObject is then applied to the legacy store's current object, which can differ from the unified object (different resourceVersions, stored fields, defaults, or a patch applied against a different base). Both writes can succeed and the stores still diverge. The same objInfo is also consumed a second time after the first UpdatedObject call.

findings.title: Delete records the object name as the kind label on storage metrics
findings.body: recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes name where every other call passes options.Kind. Each distinct object name becomes a new Prometheus label value, which creates unbounded metric cardinality and breaks per-kind dashboards and alerts.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy outcome in the storage metric
findings.body: The goroutine calls recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy), so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are counted under the storage series, and the legacy histogram is never updated for this method. It should be recordLegacyDuration.

findings.title: Unified storage failures are recorded as legacy failures
findings.body: When the storage write fails, Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The failed unified write is counted in the legacy metrics and the storage error metric is never set, so storage error rates are under-reported and legacy stats are polluted.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the request-scoped logger
findings.body: Delete builds log with name, kind and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) using the base logger. Downstream logs from the storage and legacy calls lose those fields, unlike the other methods, which pass log.

findings.title: Destroy tears down Legacy while fire-and-forget writes may still be running
findings.body: Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but background legacy goroutines may still be executing against the legacy store. Those writes then run against a destroyed backend and fail or panic. Destroy has no way to wait for in-flight legacy writes.

findings.title: Background legacy goroutines have no panic recovery
findings.body: Legacy calls used to run on the request goroutine, where net/http recovers panics per request. The bare goroutines added here have no recover, so a panic in any legacy storage method crashes the whole Grafana process instead of failing one request.

findings.title: Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write
findings.body: Storage and Legacy share a single mock.Mock, so the test cannot tell which store was called. The tests never call AssertExpectations, so the legacy expectations set up in TestMode3_Create, _Update and _DeleteCollection are never checked. Nothing verifies that Legacy is called, or with what object, which is the core of this change. The background goroutine can also call the mock after the test returns, so those calls are not observed at all.

findings.title: Legacy-side reads run immediately after writes that are now asynchronous
findings.body: In mode 3, the k8s create at line 496 returns before its legacy write completes. getFromBothAPIs then reads the legacy endpoint right away (and the legacy list comparison around line 523 does the same). These checks race the background write and will be flaky. If the legacy endpoint is actually served from unified storage, the checks do not exercise the legacy write at all. Either way the assertion does not test what it claims without waiting or polling for the legacy write.

findings.title: Test case name says List is not implemented, but it is
findings.body: The case is named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented', but List is now implemented in this PR and the case only checks that a storage error is propagated. The name is misleading to future readers.

findings.title: Create test name contradicts its setup
findings.body: The case is named 'creating an object only in the unified store', but its setup registers a legacy Create expectation and the implementation writes to legacy as well. The name describes the old behavior.

findings.title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry and unrelated checksum additions
findings.body: The line 'github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery ... /go.mod' is added a second time, duplicating the entry immediately above it. The hunk also adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporters and genproto rpc), which this dual-writer change does not touch. These look like an accidental go mod tidy or merge artifact and should be removed or verified.
